summary: This excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel (Book 11, part 12) describes Rebecca and her sister Hannah growing up on Randall's farm, where the children were free to develop on their own. Rebecca, whose growth comes from within, is seen as creative but irresponsible and is not counted as serious by her mother Aurelia, who favors Hannah. Hannah, fourteen and dependable, becomes her mother's companion in managing the household and the family's problems.
one_line: Rebecca and Hannah grow up on Randall's farm, where Rebecca's inner creativity goes unrecognized while her mother Aurelia relies on Hannah.
key_facts: Hannah lacks her sister Rebecca's... wait, Rebecca is described as lacking Hannah's patience and John's staying power, with a willfulness that makes her impatient of hard or long tasks.
The family lived at Randall's farm, where the children grew, worked, fought and educated themselves for nine months of the year, each in his own way.
Hannah was painstaking, humdrum, and limited, having been developed by forces applied from without.
Rebecca grew 'always from within outward' and needed nothing but space to develop in and a knowledge of terms to express herself.
Rebecca's forces had seemingly been set in motion when she was born and moved of their own accord, toward what no one knew, least of all Rebecca herself.

The field for Rebecca's creative instinct was painfully small, her uses including baking bread, parting Fanny's hair in varying places, and playing pranks on the children as fictitious or historical characters.
Rebecca was considered 'smart' and old for her age but was never thought superior in any way and was never counted of serious importance.
Aurelia's experience of genius, as exemplified by the deceased Lorenzo de Medici, led her to admire plain, every-day common sense.
Aurelia had to feed and clothe seven children on an income of fifteen dollars a month.
Hannah at fourteen was her mother's companion and partner in all her mother's problems and kept the house while Aurelia worked in barn and field.
Rebecca was capable of set tasks such as keeping small children from harm, feeding poultry, picking up chips, hulling strawberries and wiping dishes, but was thought irresponsible.
Aurelia, needing somebody to lean on, leaned on Hannah, who was a self-contained, well-behaved, dependable child though a trifle careworn in face and sharp in manner.
